problem.explanation: Every run is at steady state until ~TIME 100, when the transient initiates; the t0=20 window (TIME 20-70) therefore contains only the shared pre initiation plateau, which takes just 4 distinct values across all 1211 runs, channels and precision levels.

techniques.name: onset anchored jitter
techniques.oneliner: Tiny random wiggles added to the trace, starting from zero at the first step, so the window's starting point never moves.

techniques.name: excursion magnitude scaling
techniques.oneliner: The whole excursion — how far the trace travels from its start — is stretched or shrunk a little.

techniques.name: excursion magnitude warping
techniques.oneliner: The excursion is stretched unevenly along its length, more in some places and less in others, following a smooth curve.

techniques.name: shared time warping
techniques.oneliner: The window is smoothly sped up or slowed down, with the same warp on every channel so all sensors stay in step.

techniques.name: same class mixup
techniques.oneliner: Two windows of the same accident are blended together into one in between example.

techniques.name: DTW aligned pairwise averaging
techniques.oneliner: Two windows of the same accident are first lined up in time, then averaged point by point.

arms.oneliner: The plain starting point: trained on the training windows exactly as collected, nothing added.
Balancing only: the training set is topped up to the same count per class with plain copies — no new synthetic shapes.
The full recipe: every class grown to the target count with the six techniques above, then the same model trained on all of it.
A small 1D convolutional network trained on the original windows.
The same CNN trained on the augmented, balanced set.

diagnostics.label: Mean temporal range inside the window
diagnostics.oneliner: How much the signals move around inside the 60 seconds, on the study's scaled units. Bigger means the accident is visibly under way.

diagnostics.label: Between class / within class variance ratio
diagnostics.oneliner: How far apart the accident classes sit, compared with how much runs of the same accident vary. Bigger means the classes are easier to tell apart.

diagnostics.label: Mean |z(last step) − z(first step)|
diagnostics.oneliner: On average, how far the last reading has moved from the first, in standard deviation units.

diagnostics.label: Nearest centroid accuracy (full test)
diagnostics.oneliner: The simplest possible classifier — guess the class whose average window is closest — scored on the full test split.

arms.name: A0 · Baseline (12 channels)
arms.oneliner: The study's standard setup, unchanged: the 12 usual sensor channels fed to MiniRocket. The score everything else is compared against.

arms.name: A1 · Deviation from own baseline
arms.oneliner: Each window is first shifted by the run's own starting level, so only the change from normal is left. The idea: the change, not the level, should carry the news.
arms.recipe: window minus run's own baseline mean from before t0 (raw space), then study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A1b · First step anchor
arms.oneliner: Like the deviation arm, but each window is shifted by its own first reading instead of the run's starting average.
arms.recipe: window minus its own first step (raw space), then study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A1c · Raw + deviation (24 channels)
arms.oneliner: Both versions side by side — the raw window and its deviation copy, 24 channels in all — so the model can use whichever helps.
arms.recipe: 24 channels: original window ++ baseline deviation window, study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A2a · Shape features + gradient boosting
arms.oneliner: Drops the raw traces and keeps 120 simple shape numbers per window (means, spreads, slopes, ranges), read by a gradient boosting model instead of MiniRocket.
arms.recipe: 120 shape features (per channel mean/std/min/max/range/last first/slope/diff stats of scaled windows), StandardScaler, HistGradientBoosting

arms.name: A2b · Raw + differences (24 channels)
arms.oneliner: The raw window plus its step to step changes as extra channels, so any movement stands out.
arms.recipe: 24 channels: original window ++ first difference window, study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A3 · All 96 channels
arms.oneliner: Every sensor channel the simulator records, not just the usual 12 — the extra loop, everything. More information, in theory.
arms.recipe: all 96 raw channels (incl. loop-B), study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A3b · All 96 channels as deviation
arms.oneliner: All 96 channels, each one shifted by the run's own starting level.
arms.recipe: all 96 raw channels as deviation from run baseline, study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A3c · All 96 raw + deviation (192 channels)
arms.oneliner: The full 96 channels twice over — raw and deviation copies, 192 channels in all. The biggest input tried.
arms.recipe: 192 channels: expanded window ++ its baseline deviation, study preprocessing, MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A4 · Hierarchical (group first, then class)
arms.oneliner: Two steps: first guess which small group of accidents it could be, then pick inside the group. The groups came from the baseline's own confusions on held out runs.
arms.recipe: stage 1 MiniRocket+Ridge group classifier (groups from val split confusion of A0, >=3 mutual confusions), stage 2 within group MiniRocket+Ridge

arms.name: A5 · Best arm + augmentation
arms.oneliner: The best arm from the tie (the baseline) retrained on the augmented, balanced data from Experiment 1.
arms.recipe: previous run's augmentation recipe (x8 balanced, seed 2026) applied in raw space on top of A0_baseline_12ch; deviation (if any) uses the source run's baseline

arms.name: A6 · Lookup table (memoriser)
arms.oneliner: No model at all: it memorises the training windows and answers with the majority label of the identical window. A deliberate cheat that proves the point — it scores the same as every real model.
arms.recipe: exact duplicate lookup: memorise each distinct train window's majority label (fallback: global majority). A constructive proof that a trivial memoriser matches every sophisticated model.
